notes.title: Start here: a curriculum of reliability patterns
notes.body:
This repo is not an application. It is an apprenticeship curriculum: 22 short modules in `apprenticeship/curriculum/`, each teaching one engineering pattern and then pointing at worked examples in other repositories. This quest uses four of them:

1. `01-transactional-outbox.md`: changing the database and notifying something else, safely.
2. `02-idempotency.md`: what to do when the same intent arrives twice.
3. `03-concurrency-races.md`: races between concurrent requests, and optimistic concurrency.
4. `07-zero-downtime-migrations.md`: changing a schema while two app versions run.

Each module opens with a compact **Problem / pattern / checklist** section; the quiz is built from those sections. The worked traces further down cite files in other repos (for example `elirc/netopen1`), and each page says at which commit it re-read them. Those files are not in this checkout, so read the traces as illustrations rather than as code you can open here.

Read the four modules in order; each one links to the next.

excerpts.quote: Pages are short and point at **worked examples in your own repos**

readMore.why: The first module of this quest.

notes.title: Concept: two writes with no shared transaction
notes.body:
Many reliability bugs share one shape: a system must make two changes (save an order *and* tell a queue; process a message *and* record that it was processed), and nothing makes them happen together. A crash between them, a retry after a timeout, or a redelivery by the broker then produces a lost or a duplicated effect.

Read modules 01 and 02 with that shape in mind:

- In 01, list each item under **What it guarantees, and what it doesn't**, and for each one, name the failure it is about.
- Walk the **Failure-window checklist**. For every question, write the crash or race it is guarding against before reading the worked examples.
- In 02, the **Tools** are listed strongest first. For each, note who it is for (an API, a consumer, a write path) and what exactly is stored.
- Answer the four **Review questions** of 02 for any idempotency key you know.

The "second repo" section of 01 is worth reading slowly: follow one message id from the outbox to the inbox.

excerpts.quote: That is two writes with no shared transaction, so one can succeed while the other fails.

notes.title: Concept: shared state across requests and deploys
notes.body:
Modules 03 and 07 deal with the same underlying fact: more than one copy of your code touches one database at a time. In 03 the copies are concurrent requests, workers or pods; in 07 they are two versions of the app during a deploy.

For module 03:

- Read the **Problem** paragraph and explain, in your own words, how two callers can both pass the same check.
- For each entry under **Fixes, by situation**, note what the database does in that fix.
- Read **How to prove it** and decide what a test would need to assert.

For module 07:

- Read the **Problem** paragraph, then copy out **The sequence** as a numbered list, one deploy per step. Next to each step, write which app versions may be running while it is live.
- Under **Hazards that ORMs hide**, look up any statement you have not met before in the PostgreSQL documentation.

excerpts.quote: During a rolling deploy, old and new app versions run **at the same time**

notes.title: What the outbox does and does not promise
notes.body:
Writing the business change and the `OutboxMessage` row in one transaction means they commit or roll back together. Once the business write commits, its event is durable in the outbox, so it cannot be lost. That is the whole guarantee.

- *Exactly once*: a crash between publish and mark-sent republishes, so delivery is at-least-once.
- *In commit order*: ordering is only as good as the dispatcher's query (`ORDER BY` with one dispatcher, or a partition key).
- *Automatic retries with backoff*: the module says the opposite; stranded rows need a sweeper, backoff or DLQ policy you build.

excerpts.quote: Guarantees: no event is *lost* if the business write committed, because it is durable in the outbox.

notes.title: Publish, crash, publish again
notes.body:
The dispatcher's steps are: read unsent rows, publish, mark sent. If it crashes after publishing, the row is still unsent in the database. On restart the dispatcher reads it again and publishes it a second time. That is why outbox delivery is at-least-once, and why consumers must be idempotent (module 02).

- *The broker drops the copy*: a broker has no way to know the two publishes are the same row unless the consumer deduplicates.
- *Marked failed for an operator*: nothing marks it failed; it simply still looks unsent.
- *The business change rolls back*: it committed long before; the outbox only concerns delivery.

excerpts.quote: if the dispatcher crashes between *publish* and *mark sent*, it re-publishes.

notes.title: Several dispatchers must claim rows
notes.body:
If three replicas each run "select unsent rows, publish, mark sent", two of them can select the same row before either marks it, and both publish it. Checklist item 4: claim rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` (each replica locks the rows it takes and skips rows locked by others) or with a lease, so each row has one owner at a time.

- *Order by creation time*: ordering decides the sequence, not who owns a row.
- *A retry loop per publish*: retries add publishes; they do not prevent duplicates.
- *A private copy per replica*: the outbox must be written in the business transaction, so there is one table.

excerpts.quote: use `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` or a lease; otherwise messages are published twice.

notes.title: Dedup needs an id that survives republishing
notes.body:
The inbox inserts the incoming event id into a table whose only key is `Id`. A republished outbox row is turned into a new integration event built with `Guid.NewGuid()`, so its id is different every time. The inbox sees a key it has never stored, accepts it, and the consumer's effect (in the module's example, a duplicate `MeetingFee`) runs again. The fix is an id derived from something stable, such as the outbox row id.

- *Rejected because the payload matches*: the inbox compares ids, not payloads.
- *The broker replaces the older message*: brokers do not merge messages by content.
- *A unique violation*: there is no violation, because the new id is unique.

excerpts.quote: The republish carries a fresh Guid, so the inbox primary key sees a *new* message and accepts it.

notes.title: Check-then-insert races
notes.body:
"Check, then insert" runs two statements. Two requests can both run the check, both see that the key is not there, and both insert. Only the database sees every insert, so a `UNIQUE` constraint is the one shared referee: insert directly and treat the unique violation (Postgres `23505`) as "already done".

- *SELECT cannot see its own inserts*: a transaction does see its own writes; that is not the problem.
- *Postgres forbids a SELECT first*: no such rule exists.
- *Unique applies only without a prior SELECT*: a constraint is enforced on every insert, whatever came before.

notes.title: Store only answers that will not change
notes.body:
An idempotency-key store replays a stored response for a repeated key. If it stored a transient failure, such as a timeout or a 503, every retry with that key would get the same failure back, even after the problem cleared. So it should keep terminal successes, plus errors that are explicitly final. The module's worked example is a middleware that cached a 400, so retries kept replaying it.

- *Every response*: that includes transient failures, which blocks legitimate retries.
- *Errors only*: then successful requests run again, which defeats the store.
- *5xx only*: 5xx errors are the typical transient failures that must not be cached.

excerpts.quote: Only cache **terminal success** (or errors that are explicitly final).

readMore.why: The worked trace of a real idempotency middleware.

notes.title: Consumers dedup with an inbox
notes.body:
Tool 3 in the module is for consumers: an inbox or processed-message table, keyed by a **stable** message id that survives republishing. The consumer records each id it has processed and ignores ids it has seen.

- *Key store mapping keys to HTTP responses*: that is tool 2, for APIs.
- *A distributed lock*: the module lists locks for singleton jobs in module 03, not for message dedup.
- *A client key checked in a cache*: check-then-act in a cache races, and tool 1 relies on database uniqueness instead.

excerpts.quote: **An inbox/processed-message table** for consumers, keyed by a **stable message id** that survives republishing.

notes.title: Let the database check the status
notes.body:
`UPDATE ... WHERE id=@id AND status=@expected` makes the database test the status and change it in one atomic statement. The first request matches and changes one row; the second matches nothing. Checking rows-affected tells each request whether it won. (Option 2 is a concurrency token that raises a conflict for a 409 or 412.)

- *Load, then guard with an if*: both requests can read Open before either saves.
- *A unique index on status*: many tickets share a status; it would not express this rule.
- *Retry until one succeeds*: retrying a racy write does not make it safe.

excerpts.quote: run `UPDATE … WHERE id=@id AND status=@expected` and check rows-affected.

notes.title: Prove race fixes with concurrency and final state
notes.body:
A race only appears when calls overlap, so the test must fire them concurrently (`Task.WhenAll` in .NET). And a race can corrupt data while every call returns success, so the test must assert the final state: exactly one invoice, the exact balance.

- *One by one*: sequential calls never overlap, so the race cannot happen.
- *Mock the database and count saves*: the race is in the database interaction you mocked away.
- *Many runs with zero exceptions*: a lost update raises no exception at all.

excerpts.quote: write a test that fires N concurrent calls (`Task.WhenAll`) and asserts the *final state*

notes.title: Expand, then dual-write
notes.body:
The sequence is expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, stop writing old, contract, each as its own deploy. After the new column exists, the next deploy makes the new code write both old and new columns while reads stay on the old one, so any version still running sees correct data.

- *Backfill in the migration transaction*: backfill is step 3, and it runs from a throttled job, explicitly not inside the migration transaction.
- *Switch every read at once*: switching reads is step 4, ideally behind a flag.
- *Drop the old column*: that is the final contract step, after a full release.

excerpts.quote: **Dual-write:** the new code writes both old and new; reads stay on the old.

notes.title: Keep the column for a rollback
notes.body:
During and after a deploy, the previous app version may run again: a rollback brings it back. That version still reads the old column. Waiting one full release after the code stops writing it keeps rollback safe (the module calls this N-1 compatibility); only then is the column dropped.

- *Time for the backfill*: the backfill happened at step 3, before reads switched.
- *Rebuilding indexes*: dropping a column does not wait on index rebuilds; that is not the reason given.
- *Regenerating ORM models*: models are part of the code release, not something the database waits for.

excerpts.quote: wait one full release so rollback stays safe (N-1 compatibility)

notes.title: CONCURRENTLY, outside a transaction
notes.body:
A plain `CREATE INDEX` in PostgreSQL blocks writes to the table while it builds. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` builds without blocking writes, at the cost of a slower build, and PostgreSQL refuses to run it inside a transaction block. The migration therefore issues it on its own, not inside the usual migration transaction.

- *Plain CREATE INDEX in the migration*: it locks out writes for the whole build.
- *CONCURRENTLY inside a transaction*: Postgres raises an error for that.
- *Postgres never blocks writes*: a plain index build does block them.

excerpts.quote: Index builds lock writes unless you run `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` (Postgres)
